notes.meaning: The psalmist asks God not to stay quiet or hold back from helping. When enemies threaten, it can feel as if God is silent, but believers may freely ask Him to step in. Faith calls on God to answer their prayers and show His power through action.

The attacking nations are shouting loudly and proudly raising their heads in defiance. Because God chose Israel as His own, their enemies are also His enemies. Those who oppose God's people are really setting themselves against God Himself.

The enemies make clever, secret plans against God's people. The psalmist calls the people God's cherished or hidden ones because the Lord shelters them like a precious treasure. No human scheme can succeed against those whom God protects.

The hostile nations openly plot to wipe out Israel completely so that the nation is never remembered again. They do not merely want to defeat Israel in battle; they want to erase God's people from the earth. Evil often tries to destroy the worship of the true God entirely.

The nations put aside their own rivalries to unite with one heart against Israel. They have cut a treaty, swearing together to accomplish their goal. When wicked forces join hands against God's people, they are making a pact against God Himself.

Ten nations surrounding Israel unite in this coalition, from Edom and the desert tribes to Philistia and Tyre, backed by the distant power of Assyria. The descendants of Lot, Moab and Ammon, appear to lead the alliance with the support of their neighbors. The psalmist names them all before God, trusting the Lord when dangers surround His people on every side.

The psalm asks God to repeat the great victories of the past, like the defeat of Midian under Gideon and the fall of Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon River. Those ancient armies were crushed and left unburied to rot like waste on the ground. Remembering how God rescued His people in the past gives believers confidence in present trials.

The prayer asks that the leaders of the new coalition meet the same end as Midian's generals, Oreb and Zeeb, and its kings, Zebah and Zalmunna. God brought down those proud rulers when they tried to crush Israel. No human ruler is too powerful for God to humble.

The invading armies boasted that they would take the homes and pastures of God for their own use. They saw the land of Israel as an easy prize to seize. But the land belonged to the Lord, so their greed was a direct attack on God's property.

The psalmist asks God to scatter the enemy like rolling tumbleweeds or lightweight chaff blown away by the wind. Though they think they are strong and firmly rooted, before God they are helpless and unstable. God can blow away the proudest armies in a moment.

The prayer asks God to pursue the enemies like a wildfire roaring through mountain brush and a terrifying storm sweeping across the land. These pictures show how swiftly and completely God's judgment can overtake those who do evil. Nothing can stand in the path of the Lord's power.

The psalmist asks God to cover the attackers with the shame of defeat so that they will turn and seek the Lord. The goal of this plea is not merely revenge, but the humbling of proud enemies so they might seek the true God. God often uses difficulty to lead people to recognize their need of Him.

If the enemies refuse to turn to God, the psalmist asks that their plots end in lasting defeat and disgrace. Those who persist in fighting against God will find only ruin in the end. Stubborn rebellion against the Lord always leads to failure.

The final purpose of God's victory is that all nations may know that the Lord alone is the Most High over all the earth. God delivers His people so His supreme rule will be honored by everyone. True prayer always looks beyond our own safety to God's ultimate glory.
